, alluded to in this chapter, Lucifer thought he could do a better job than God and sought to overthrow Him. But he failed and was banished from Heaven. Instead of asking for forgiveness he turns his back on God anyway and refuses to serve Him to preserve his own pride.

Stephen believes that to become a good artist one must remove oneself from all ties. The Catholic church is one of the strongest and most influential ties to anyone growing up in early 20th century Ireland, so Stephen’s defiance is just like Lucifer’s defiance, and just like Lucifer Stephen ‘will not serve’. children: This part of Chapter 3 comes just after Stephen Dedalus has a casual encounter with a prostitute for the first time. It seems almost too coincidental that he is now exhibiting signs of gluttony in the way he is longing for large amounts of food. Both of these situations feature one of the seven deadly sins recognized by the Christian church, and they depict Stephen’s descent from the graces of God into the world of sin. Both of these sins can be characterized by the temptation they cause in Stephen as he is reluctant to make a move on the prostitute at first, but eventually succumbs. Similarly, it can be argued that Stephen’s hunger causes him to fetishize food in a sinful manner.

annotatable.link_title: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (Chap. 3) by James Joyce
annotatable.title: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (Chap. 3)

children: In order to demonstrate the development of Stephen’s consciousness Joyce ends each chapter with an epiphany. Stephen recognizes the delusion of one way of life and recognizes the truth of another. In this moment Stephen understands that he must turn to a religious life. Unlike other novels where the narrators look back at the events of their childhood with an adult outlook, Portrait takes up a different style. When Stephen declares, “Another life!” and “The past was past,” we are given no hints that Stephen’s religious life will eventually be replaced by his artistic life. Rather, much like Stephen, we are led to believe that he will remain religious for the rest of his life. In this sense, we experience the successive epiphanies in Stephen’s life just as he experiences them.

children: Overall this is a powerful depiction of the concept of transubstantiation, which is the idea that the Communion wafer isn’t just a metaphor for the body of Christ, but it really is in essence the body of Christ. At this moment, Stephen believes that this sacrament will save him from his past life. Later in Chapter Five Stephen draws again upon transubstantiation, this time as a metaphor for art.
